lesson.subject: Maths
lesson.lo: To multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number using partitioning
lesson.displayedLo: To multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number
lesson.stickingPoint: The tens digit treated as a digit rather than a number of tens: either the zero is dropped (30 × 4 = 12) or the two digit products are written side by side (28 × 3 = 624) instead of added.

teacherOrientation: Teacher orientation: Children multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number by partitioning it into tens and ones, multiplying each part and adding the two answers. The starter warms up the table facts and the partitioning they already have, then one short board explanation with base-ten rods shows why 20 × 3 is six tens. You model 23 × 3 and then 28 × 3 on a part-whole model with the working written beside it, guide the class through 32 × 4 and 47 × 5, and they do five on their own in books. They then judge a wrong claim (34 × 4 = 1216) and finish on two word problems. The tricky move is the tens part: 30 × 4 is 3 tens × 4 = 12 tens, which is 120, and the two slips to watch are writing 12 instead of 120, and writing the two digit answers side by side (3 × 4 = 12, 4 × 4 = 16, so "1216"). The tens step is taught on the slide straight after the vocabulary card, and the side-by-side slip is named out loud in your second modelled example.

speakerNotes.script: Say to children: Five quick ones to wake your brains up. The first three are table facts you know. The last two are partitioning, and you can do that in your sleep: split the number into its tens and its ones. Off you go, and we'll check them in three minutes.
speakerNotes.teacherInfo: The brief names 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 as the fluent tables, and the lesson only ever multiplies by those. Both skills here are used inside every question today.

misconceptions.belief: You can multiply each digit and write the two answers side by side, so 28 × 3 = 624.
misconceptions.correctiveFact: The 2 in 28 is 2 tens, so its answer is 60, and 60 is added to 24 to make 84.
misconceptions.strategy: Named out loud in the My Turn script on the second example (28 × 3), where it first gives a wrong answer, then retested once as Ava's claim (34 × 4 = 1216) in the practise beat with the star fact off the slide.
misconceptions.reason: It gives the right answer on 23 × 3 and the wrong one on 28 × 3, so it survives easy examples and only fails when the ones product is two digits. Children need to see it fail and say why.

misconceptions.correctiveFact: 20 is 2 tens, so 20 × 3 is 6 tens, which is 60.
misconceptions.strategy: Taught head-on in the prepare beat with base-ten rods, carried as the star fact through the cycle, watched for in the Our Turn on 30 × 4, and retested on the worksheet as Sam's claim (40 × 3 = 12).
misconceptions.reason: Multiplying a multiple of ten is not in the stated prior learning, and using the bare table fact is the predictable slip when the tens product reaches 12 tens or more.

concepts.name: Multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number by partitioning

teachingSequence.label: Multiplying tens
teachingSequence.unlocks: They can multiply a multiple of ten by a one-digit number (20 × 3 = 60), which the tens step of every example needs.
teachingSequence.thinking: Why does 2 × 3 tell me what 20 × 3 is?

content.activity:
20 × 3

20 is 2 tens. So 20 × 3 is 2 tens × 3.
2 × 3 = 6, so 2 tens × 3 = 6 tens.
6 tens is 60. So 20 × 3 = 60.

speakerNotes.script: Say to children: Right, before the new bit, there's one thing we need. What's 2 × 3? Six. Now look at these rods. Each rod is a ten. Here's twenty: two tens. And I've got three lots of twenty. Count the rods with me. Two, four, six. Six rods, and every rod is a ten. So 2 tens × 3 is 6 tens, and 6 tens is 60. That's all 20 × 3 is: the fact you already know, 2 × 3, but the answer is in tens. Try this one in your head. 30 × 4. Three tens times four. 3 × 4 is 12, so that's 12 tens. And 12 tens is... 120. Not 12. That's the one to be careful with, because once the table answer gets to 10 or more, 12 tens looks like it could just be 12. It's 120. That's our star fact and it's staying on the board.
speakerNotes.teacherInfo: The predictable slip is 30 × 4 = 12: the child uses the table fact and forgets the answer is in tens. The star fact is the reference for the rest of the lesson and comes off only for Ava's claim later.

teachingSequence.label: My Turn
teachingSequence.unlocks: They have seen the whole method run twice: partition, multiply each part, add, which the Our Turn has them direct themselves.

speakerNotes.script: Say to children: 23 × 3. I could count 23 three times, but there's a better way, and it starts with something you can already do. I partition 23. 23 is 20 and 3, so I write 20 in this part and 3 in this part. Now, instead of one hard multiplication, I've got two easy ones. First the tens. 20 × 3. That's 2 tens × 3, which is 6 tens. 60. I'll write it: 20 × 3 = 60. Now the ones. 3 × 3 = 9. Written down. And last, I add my two answers. 60 + 9 = 69. So 23 × 3 = 69. Partition, times the tens, times the ones, add them up. Same again, with one thing different. 28 × 3. Partition: 20 and 8. Tens: 20 × 3 = 60, same as before. Ones: 8 × 3 = 24. Now stop and look at this. Some people see the 6 and the 24 and write 624. That's not a real answer, and here's why. That 6 isn't a six, it's 60. I'm not sticking my two answers next to each other, I'm adding them. 60 + 24 = 84. 28 × 3 = 84. Look at the four steps on the side: that's exactly what I did, both times, and they're what you'll use.
speakerNotes.teacherInfo: The two examples hold the multiplier and the tens still; only the ones digit changes, so the ones product becoming two digits is the one new thing, and it is where the side-by-side answer first shows.

teachingSequence.label: Our Turn
teachingSequence.unlocks: They have directed the method themselves on numbers whose tens product passes 100, which the Your Turn then asks of them alone.
teachingSequence.thinking: Which part am I multiplying now, and is the answer in tens or in ones?

speakerNotes.script: Say to children: Your turn to tell me what to do. 32 × 4. What's the first step? Partition. What's 32 partitioned? 30 and 2. Which part do we multiply first? The tens. So what's 30 × 4? Think in tens: 3 tens × 4. 12 tens. So what do I write, 12 or 120? 120. What's next? The ones: 2 × 4 = 8. And now? Add them. 120 + 8 = 128. Next one, and this one's a bit bigger. 47 × 5. Partition it for me. 40 and 7. Tens: 40 × 5. Four tens times five, so how many tens? 20 tens. And what's 20 tens? 200. Ones: 7 × 5 = 35. Add: 200 + 35 = 235. Before you go off on your own, tell your partner the four steps without looking at the board.
speakerNotes.teacherInfo: Both examples cross 100 on the tens step on purpose: it is the case the My Turn did not show, and it is where 12 tens gets written as 12.
speakerNotes.lookFor: Look for: 30 × 4 given as 12; the two answers added rather than placed side by side.

teachingSequence.label: Your Turn
teachingSequence.unlocks: They can run the method alone, which Ava's claim and the word problems both draw on.
teachingSequence.thinking: What are the two smaller multiplications hiding inside this one, and have I added both answers?

content.activityArchitecture: Core action: run the partition method alone, five times, in books, drawing their own part-whole model and writing the two multiplications and the add for each. Variation, one feature at a time: (1) clean case, (2) ones product two digits, (3) tens product over 100, (4) both together with a zero in the sum, (5) the 8 table with both. Instances stand separately, each with its own working.

content.activity: Reasoning: inspect an attempt. Children judge a wrong claim built on the side-by-side rule on a number the class has not seen, decide alone, tell a partner, then write one sentence saying what has actually happened.
content.format: Own decision first, then partner talk, then one written sentence explaining the mistake.
content.task:
Ava says: "34 × 4 = 1216, because 3 × 4 = 12 and 4 × 4 = 16."

Is Ava right? Explain your answer.

speakerNotes.script: Say to children: Ava has had a go at 34 × 4 and she's got 1216. Thirty-four lots of four, and the answer's over a thousand? Have a think on your own first: is Ava right, and how do you know? Then tell your partner. Then write me one sentence that says what's actually happened. If you're stuck, partition 34 and do it properly, then compare your answer with hers.
speakerNotes.teacherInfo: This is the side-by-side error from the My Turn on a fresh number. The star fact is deliberately off this slide so the child has to supply 30 × 4 = 120 themselves.

activityArchitecture.coreActionAndEvidence: Run the partition method on fresh two-digit by one-digit multiplications, showing the partition, the two multiplications and the add; judge one dropped-zero attempt; find the multiplication in two one-step stories.
activityArchitecture.amount: Four fluency calculations, one claim to judge, two word problems: seven performances of the method.
activityArchitecture.variationAndBoundaryPlan: Fluency climbs through the taught cases: ones product one digit, tens product over 100, ones product two digits, both together. The reasoning item retests the dropped zero (40 × 3 = 12). Word problems use multipliers 5 and 3. No number repeats a deck example.
activityArchitecture.organisation: Fluency first, the first two questions in the board's own form (part-whole with the whole filled and parts blank, three working lines beside), the next two bare with working room; then Reasoning; then Problem Solving. Each question stands separately with its own working.

vocabularyIntroductions.script: Say to children: One word before we start, and you've already used it this morning. Partition. When you split 64 into 60 and 4, that's partitioning: breaking a number into its tens and its ones. Look at the picture. 23 at the top, and the two parts underneath it, 20 and 3. Today every single question starts with a partition, because it turns one big multiplication into two small ones you already know.
